doc.title: Tony Parenti and Anthony Sbarbaro Interview, 1959-06-29

title: Sidney Arodin in Denver and Carmichael's tune purchase
summary: Parenti last saw Arodin in distress; Carmichael bought a tune from him; Provenzano and a cotton-mill boss are recalled.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I was I saw Sydney was out in Denver Colorado and had to be in the 20s I haven't seen that boy since last time I saw him was under very distressing condition I was down near all of us at the time when I was with Ted Lewis you know yeah and I made a little wrong somebody told me we playing in a little club around and I don't even remember the name of the club but I went in there and Sydney's got the little group he's front of it and my gracious alive here is he alive? he was there no he hasn't passed away but he was there with this little group and he didn't huddle about what to play and it was a big technical discussion thing about this and that and then he played things like that I think he was mentally disturbed a little bit by then evidently because after we got through he took me back at a long we had a jog we had a little gin there and I drank with him but there's a boy that's a shame I'll tell you as long as you brought the name up I might mention the fact that when I was in Florida not more than five or six years ago up there playing uh Hoagie Carmichael came down there in those golf tournaments and came down to the little club where I was flying there with this Dixieland band and we got in a huddle down on the table between the missions and I've known Hoagie on and off for quite a length of time he knew that I was from the all and so he says to me Tony he says do you know the address of Sydney Aragon well I say stuff he is not living yet. He says, I know that. He says, I'd love to do a little good turn for the family. And during the conversation, it was brought up to the extent where he had bought this tune from Sidney Aaron and Appalachian. And he had bought this tune from Sidney for $100. And of course, you have no idea how much money he has made on that tune. Let's let alone just the royalties alone. I mean, one of these outstanding heads, but he had wanted to do something. So I, during the course of the time that I was there, I got the address and I gave it to him before he left. So he evidently might have sent the check on his family, which I thought was a nice gesture. That's a good sign, man. You remember clarinet player that nobody ever remembered? And he didn't make too much of a part of a established name value. But he was from New Orleans and I knew him very well because I went to school with him. He was also part of the Italian band. And he finally wound up playing jazz to the degree. And he finally went to Chicago and worked for some place in Cicero for, until something happened, he died. His name was John Provincana. Oh yeah. Clarinet player. Well, I know the Provincana trumpet player. Johnny Provincana. I don't know about, I don't know if it was a clarinet player. Well, I don't know about his name. Johnny Provincana too. That's a funny thing. And he was a little cock-eyed, this fellow. A little cross-need out. I know who you mean. to one thing I love and he was a little cock-eyed this one no cross I know who you mean is that I'll tell you who used to be my boss and the Guinness of the cotton mill this I'm a kid pulled by the name of Joe he had gold those days go all in his mouth you know this guy's got that too oh no I was a little bit yeah yeah he's uh but he was my boss in the cotton mill who's my flower I don't know Mike well he's terrible he's young oh my hair talk
